lines.text: Every structure so far answered one question: is this key actually here.
This one answers a completely different question. Where does it rank, among everything else that's here too — for almost nothing extra.
Here's the one new thing: a count, kept at every node, of how big its own slice of the tree actually is.
Nothing about the keys changed. Every node just started keeping track of how much sits underneath it.
An insert just landed somewhere in this tree.
Think about it before the reveal: that one new key can't be free. Something has to pay for it in bookkeeping, and not everywhere.
Every node the insert actually walked past on its way down — nothing else.
Each one of those nodes just gained exactly one new thing underneath it. Nothing off that path gained anything at all.
That walk down wasn't extra work. It's the same walk the insert needed anyway, just to find where the key belonged.
So the counting hitches a ride on something the tree was already doing. Nothing underneath gets re-scanned, and nothing outside that one path even notices.
Here's the payoff. Want the middle key, or the tenth-smallest, or whichever rank you like?
Compare it against the left side's count. Too big, subtract that count and go right. Too small, go left. Land exactly on it, and you're done.
Now the harder question. A rotation just relinked two nodes.
Guess at the damage before you see it: does fixing the bookkeeping here spread far, or stay small?
Exactly two — the two nodes that just changed which one is whose parent.
Every other node in this tree still has precisely the same set of things underneath it that it had a moment ago. Nothing else moved.
Watch it happen: two parents swap places, and exactly two counts get recomputed.
This looked like it should disturb a lot of bookkeeping. It disturbs exactly two numbers, every single time.
Here's why that's not a coincidence about this one count in particular.
This count survives a rotation cheaply because it's built from nothing but a node and its own two children. Any count built that same way survives a rotation the same way, at the same tiny cost.
Rank runs the opposite direction: start at a key, and climb.
Every time that climb comes up from a right-side child, add the whole left side's count to your running total. By the time you reach the top, that total is the key's own rank.
Everything in this topic gets checked right here, not just drawn.
A query asking for a specific rank never needs more comparisons than the tree is tall.
And one real rotation, measured directly: exactly two of these counts actually change.
